relatedConcept: The Task tool is the spawning mechanism for subagents, and it must appear in the coordinator's allowedTools for any delegation to be possible.
overallExplanation: Subagents are spawned via the Task tool, so the coordinator's allowedTools must include "Task". Perfectly defined subagents are unreachable if the coordinator lacks the one tool that invokes them — it will silently attempt all work itself.

objective: Configure subagent invocation, context passing, and spawning
question: Your search subagents return findings as flowing prose in which claims and their source mentions are interleaved ("...as one industry analysis noted, adoption doubled, though a separate survey from last spring suggests..."). Two handoffs later, the synthesis subagent's report attaches citations to the wrong claims and drops several sources entirely. What change to the context-passing design fixes this?
options: Instruct the synthesis subagent to double-check every citation against the original sources before finalizing the report

Require subagents to emit findings in a structured format that separates content from metadata — each claim paired with its source URL, document name, and page number — so attribution survives every handoff intact
Include the full raw text of every retrieved web page in the synthesis subagent's prompt so it can re-derive correct citations itself
Add a PostToolUse hook on the coordinator that appends an alphabetized bibliography of all retrieved sources to each subagent handoff
optionExplanations: The synthesis agent cannot verify against sources it does not have: it received prose in which claim-source pairings were already ambiguous, and no instruction can recover bindings that were never explicitly represented. Verification requires the structure this pipeline lacks.

Correct. Structured data formats that separate content from metadata — source URLs, document names, page numbers attached to each individual finding — are the prescribed way to pass context between agents while preserving attribution. Prose interleaving makes claim-source bindings implicit, and every summarization step degrades implicit bindings further.

Raw page dumps explode the synthesis agent's context with material the search and analysis stages already processed, and re-deriving citations from scratch duplicates their work while inviting new mismatches. The pipeline needs bindings preserved, not evidence re-litigated.

A detached bibliography lists sources without binding them to claims — the report still cannot say which claim came from which source. The failure is per-claim attribution, and an appended list at the handoff level does not represent that relationship at all.
principle: structure separates claims from source metadata at every handoff
relatedConcept: Passing context between agents in structured formats — content distinct from source URLs, document names, page numbers — is what preserves attribution across multi-agent pipelines.
overallExplanation: Use structured data formats that separate content from metadata, pairing each finding with its source URL, document name, and page number. Prose interleaving leaves claim-source bindings implicit, and they corrupt a little more at every handoff.

objective: Configure subagent invocation, context passing, and spawning
question: Your coordinator's delegation prompts read like scripts: "Open the document. Read section 2. Extract the table on page 4. Then summarize paragraphs 6 through 9." Subagents perform flawlessly on the document layouts the scripts anticipate and fail badly on anything else — skipping content when a section is renumbered or a table moves. How should the delegation prompts be redesigned?
options: Specify the research goal and the quality criteria the output must meet, letting each subagent adapt its own approach to whatever document structure it actually encounters
Extend each script with conditional branches covering every document variant the team has encountered so far, updating the scripts as new layouts appear
Have the coordinator read each document itself first and generate a bespoke step-by-step script tailored to that document's exact layout before delegating
Lower the subagents' sampling temperature so they follow the procedural instructions more literally and deviate less from the prescribed steps
optionExplanations: Correct. Coordinator prompts should specify research goals and quality criteria rather than step-by-step procedural instructions, precisely to enable subagent adaptability. A goal like "extract the reported quarterly figures with their reporting periods; every figure must cite its page" survives any layout, because the subagent — an LLM with the document in front of it — decides how to achieve it.

Variant-by-variant branching is an arms race against document diversity that the team never wins: each new layout fails first, then gets a patch. It also makes prompts enormous while keeping the core defect — the subagent is forbidden from using its own judgment.

This makes the coordinator do every subagent's reading work up front, destroying the delegation benefit and doubling document processing. The coordinator's context fills with layouts it should never need, and the bespoke scripts still break when a document surprises the script-writer.

Temperature adjusts sampling variability, not comprehension of instructions, and stricter literalism is the opposite of the fix: the failures happen because the scripts are followed literally against documents they do not describe. More obedience to a wrong script produces more wrong extractions.
principle: delegate goals and quality criteria, not procedures
relatedConcept: Coordinator prompts that state research goals and quality criteria — instead of step-by-step scripts — let subagents adapt to whatever they actually encounter.
overallExplanation: Delegation prompts should specify research goals and quality criteria rather than step-by-step procedures, enabling subagents to adapt to real-world variation. Scripts fail on every layout their author did not anticipate; goals survive them all.

objective: Configure subagent invocation, context passing, and spawning
question: You are adding a new document-analysis subagent type to your Agent SDK research system and writing its AgentDefinition. A teammate unfamiliar with the SDK asks what this configuration actually provides. Which two elements are genuinely part of what an AgentDefinition configures for a subagent type? (Choose two.)
options: A description of the subagent's purpose, which the coordinator uses to decide when this subagent type is the right one to invoke
A memory-sharing flag that, when enabled, lets the subagent read the coordinator's conversation history directly during execution
An inheritance setting that automatically passes the parent agent's accumulated context into the subagent at spawn time
A system prompt establishing the subagent's role, plus tool restrictions that scope it to the tools its specialization requires
optionExplanations: Correct. AgentDefinition includes a description of each subagent type, and that description is what informs delegation decisions — the coordinator matches the task at hand against subagent descriptions when choosing which specialist to spawn via the Task tool.

No such flag exists. Subagents operate with isolated context and do not share memory with the coordinator or between invocations; anything the subagent needs must be explicitly included in the prompt it is spawned with. Isolation is fundamental, not a toggle.

This is the same misconception in different clothing: subagents do not automatically inherit parent context, and no AgentDefinition setting changes that. Context passing is an explicit act — the coordinator writes findings into the delegation prompt itself.

Correct. AgentDefinition configures each subagent type's system prompt — establishing role and behavior — and its tool restrictions, so a document-analysis agent gets document tools and nothing that invites cross-specialization misuse. Description, system prompt, and tool restrictions are the definition's substance.
principle: AgentDefinition = description, system prompt, tool restrictions
relatedConcept: AgentDefinition configures descriptions, system prompts, and tool restrictions per subagent type — context isolation is fundamental and no setting disables it.
overallExplanation: AgentDefinition provides each subagent type's description (guiding the coordinator's invocation decisions), system prompt, and tool restrictions. Memory-sharing flags and automatic context inheritance do not exist — subagent context is always passed explicitly in the delegation prompt.

objective: Implement multi-step workflows with enforcement and handoff patterns
question: After a prerequisite gate on refunds eliminated a compliance problem, your team is energized and proposes gating every workflow ordering programmatically: greeting before lookup, empathy statement before any fix, summary before session close. Three sprints later the agent is brittle — legitimate conversation variations get blocked, and the gate code is a maintenance burden. What principle should govern where enforcement is applied?
options: Gate every ordering rule programmatically, since deterministic enforcement is categorically superior to prompt guidance and the brittleness just needs more engineering

Reserve programmatic enforcement for rules that require deterministic compliance — such as identity verification before financial operations — and use prompt-based guidance for soft ordering preferences where a small failure rate is acceptable
Remove all gates including the refund prerequisite and consolidate every rule into a carefully engineered system prompt for consistency of mechanism
Replace the gates with a second Claude instance that reviews each proposed tool call against the full rulebook before permitting it to execute
optionExplanations: Universal gating mistakes the lesson of the refund win: that gate succeeded because the rule was a hard invariant with financial consequences. Conversational orderings have legitimate exceptions by nature, so encoding them as absolutes guarantees the observed brittleness — no amount of engineering makes a soft preference hard.

Correct. The enforcement spectrum matches mechanism to consequence: programmatic prerequisites where prompt instructions' non-zero failure rate is unacceptable (identity checks before financial operations), and prompt guidance for stylistic or soft-ordering preferences where occasional deviation is harmless. This keeps gates few, meaningful, and maintainable while the agent stays flexible.

This overcorrects into the original compliance failure: prompt instructions have a non-zero failure rate, and the refund prerequisite exists precisely because that rate was unacceptable for financial operations. Uniformity of mechanism is not a virtue worth reintroducing unauthorized refunds for.

A reviewing model is still probabilistic — it can approve a violating call — while adding a full inference round-trip of latency and cost to every tool call in the system. For hard rules it under-delivers versus a simple gate; for soft preferences it is wildly disproportionate.
principle: gates for hard invariants, prompts for soft preferences
relatedConcept: Programmatic enforcement and prompt-based guidance are complementary: deterministic compliance requirements get gates; stylistic ordering preferences tolerate probabilistic adherence.
overallExplanation: Reserve programmatic enforcement for rules needing deterministic compliance — like verification before financial operations — and use prompt guidance for soft preferences where small failure rates are acceptable. Gating everything makes agents brittle; gating nothing reopens compliance holes.

objective: Implement multi-step workflows with enforcement and handoff patterns
question: When your support agent escalates a billing dispute mid-investigation, the human billing specialists — who work in a separate ticketing system with no access to the agent's conversation — currently receive only a ticket ID and a sentiment label like "customer frustrated". Specialists re-contact customers to ask for basics, and escalated-case resolution time has doubled. What should the escalation carry instead?
options: The complete raw conversation transcript exported verbatim into the ticket, so specialists can reconstruct the investigation from primary material
A deep link back into the agent's session plus a one-paragraph abstract, so specialists can pull details on demand as questions arise
The sentiment trajectory across the conversation and the agent's confidence score, so specialists can triage which escalations deserve attention first

A structured handoff summary containing customer details, the root cause analysis so far, the disputed amount, and the agent's recommended action, so the specialist can act immediately without re-investigating
optionExplanations: A raw multi-turn transcript buries the actionable facts in greetings, tool chatter, and dead-end turns — the specialist must re-perform the agent's analysis to find the root cause. It transfers data while failing to transfer the investigation's conclusions, which is what saves resolution time.

The premise of this scenario is that specialists work in a separate system without access to the agent's conversation, so the link resolves to nothing they can open. Even with access, on-demand pulling recreates the re-investigation burden the handoff should eliminate.

Sentiment and confidence describe the conversation's mood, not the case: a specialist triaging by frustration level still opens the ticket knowing nothing about who the customer is, what went wrong, or what amount is disputed. The doubled resolution time comes from missing substance, not missing prioritization.

Correct. Structured handoff protocols for mid-process escalation carry exactly this payload: customer details, root cause analysis, the amounts involved, and recommended actions. The specialist inherits the investigation's conclusions rather than its raw material, and can act on the case immediately — the specific fix for humans who lack transcript access.
principle: hand off conclusions and recommendations, not mood or raw logs
relatedConcept: Structured handoff summaries — customer details, root cause, amounts, recommended action — are the escalation payload for humans without conversation access.
overallExplanation: Escalations to transcript-less humans need a structured handoff summary: customer details, root cause analysis, disputed amounts, and recommended actions. Sentiment labels and raw transcripts both force the specialist to re-investigate, which is what doubles resolution time.

objective: Implement multi-step workflows with enforcement and handoff patterns
question: You implemented a programmatic prerequisite gate that blocks process_refund until get_customer has returned a verified customer ID. It works — no unverified refunds occur — but the gate silently swallows blocked calls, so the agent perceives process_refund as broken, apologizes to the customer, and gives up on cases it could have completed after verifying. How should the gate behave when it blocks a call?
options: Return a structured response explaining that customer verification is required first, so the agent can call get_customer, complete verification, and legitimately retry the refund
Continue failing silently by design, since revealing the gate's existence teaches the model to anticipate and possibly reason its way around the enforcement
Terminate the automated workflow and escalate every blocked refund attempt to a human agent, since a blocked call indicates the model cannot be trusted on this case
Detect the block, execute get_customer automatically inside the gate using the details the customer already stated, and then allow the original refund call to proceed
optionExplanations: Correct. A gate's job is to enforce ordering, not to strand the workflow: returning a structured explanation converts the block into a recoverable step, steering the agent to perform verification and then retry legitimately. Enforcement stays deterministic while the agent keeps its ability to complete the case — the compliance win without the abandonment cost.

Silence cannot strengthen a programmatic gate — the gate blocks regardless of what the model knows — so opacity buys nothing. What it costs is visible in production: the agent misdiagnoses a policy block as a system fault, misleads the customer about an outage, and abandons resolvable cases.

Escalating every blocked call confuses a sequencing correction with an unresolvable case: the agent is fully capable of verifying and then refunding. Routing these to humans forfeits first-contact resolution on routine refunds and floods specialists with cases that needed one more tool call.

Auto-executing verification with customer-stated details defeats the check's purpose: verification exists because stated identity cannot be trusted, and it may require interaction — asking for additional identifiers — that only the agent can conduct. The gate would be laundering unverified data into a verified-looking flow.
principle: a blocking gate should redirect the agent to the prerequisite
relatedConcept: Prerequisite gates enforce ordering best when a block returns structured guidance, letting the agent complete the missing step and retry rather than abandoning the case.
overallExplanation: When a prerequisite gate blocks a call, it should return a structured response naming the missing prerequisite so the agent can verify and retry. Silent blocking preserves compliance but destroys resolution — the agent misreads policy enforcement as system failure.

objective: Implement multi-step workflows with enforcement and handoff patterns
question: Your team is triaging a requirements backlog for the customer support agent, deciding which behaviors get programmatic enforcement and which are handled through prompt guidance. Budget allows building enforcement for only two items this quarter. Which two requirements genuinely need programmatic enforcement rather than prompt instructions? (Choose two.)
options: The agent should acknowledge the customer's frustration before proposing a resolution on emotionally charged tickets
No refund may ever be processed until get_customer has returned a verified customer identity for the session
Refunds above the compliance policy threshold must never execute autonomously and must always route to a human approver
Responses should stay concise, avoid internal jargon, and close by asking whether anything else is needed
optionExplanations: This is a tone preference with no compliance consequence when occasionally missed — a customer receiving a solution slightly before the empathy statement suffers no harm. Prompt guidance with examples handles it well, and a gate here would block legitimate conversational variation.

Correct. Identity verification before financial operations is the canonical deterministic-compliance requirement: prompt instructions carry a non-zero failure rate, and a single unverified refund is a real financial and compliance loss. A programmatic prerequisite that blocks process_refund until verification completes is the only guarantee.

Correct. A hard monetary threshold with a mandatory human-approval path is a business rule requiring guaranteed compliance — an interception mechanism that blocks over-threshold refund calls and redirects to escalation makes violations impossible, which auditors require and prompts cannot promise.

Style and closing-question conventions are probabilistic-compliance territory: occasional lapses cost nothing measurable, and enforcement machinery for phrasing would be brittle and unmaintainable. This is exactly what system prompt guidance is for.
principle: spend enforcement budget where violations have hard consequences
relatedConcept: Deterministic enforcement belongs to rules whose single violation is unacceptable — verification prerequisites and monetary thresholds — while tone and style ride on prompt guidance.
overallExplanation: Programmatic enforcement belongs to the two hard invariants: verification before any refund, and the monetary threshold above which refunds must route to humans. Tone acknowledgment and response style tolerate the small failure rate of prompt guidance.

objective: Apply Agent SDK hooks for tool call interception and data normalization
question: Your Agent SDK deployment has two new requirements: (a) results returned by a records-lookup MCP tool sometimes contain unmasked personal data that must never reach the model, and (b) any write_config call whose environment argument is "production" must be prevented from executing. An engineer asks which hook pattern applies to each requirement. What is the correct pairing?
options: Use PostToolUse hooks for both requirements, since the post-execution hook observes the most complete information about each tool interaction
Intercept outgoing tool calls for both requirements, since acting before execution is strictly safer than acting after it
Intercept outgoing tool calls to block production write_config before it executes, and use a PostToolUse hook to redact personal data from results before the model processes them
Handle both requirements with system prompt instructions, since hook code adds latency to every tool interaction in the deployment
optionExplanations: PostToolUse fires after the tool has run, which is fatal for requirement (b): by the time the hook observes the call, production configuration has already been written. Post-execution observation can transform or audit results, but it cannot prevent an action that already happened.

Pre-execution interception cannot satisfy requirement (a): the personal data lives in the tool's result, which does not exist until after execution. A hook inspecting the outgoing call sees arguments, not the response — there is nothing to redact yet.

Correct. The two hook patterns map to the two halves of a tool interaction: interception of outgoing calls enforces rules about whether an action may execute (block production write_config, arguments in hand, before anything happens), while PostToolUse transforms results before the model processes them (redact personal data on the way in). Matching hook point to purpose is the core skill.

Both requirements demand deterministic guarantees — personal data must never reach the model, production writes must never execute — and prompt instructions provide probabilistic compliance at best. A prompt also cannot redact data at all: the result reaches the model's context in order to be read.
principle: gate actions before execution; transform results after it
relatedConcept: Hook selection follows the interaction lifecycle — outgoing-call interception for blocking and compliance, PostToolUse for transforming results before the model sees them.
overallExplanation: Block-or-allow decisions belong in hooks that intercept outgoing tool calls, before execution; data transformation and redaction belong in PostToolUse hooks, before the model processes results. Each requirement fails if assigned to the other hook point.

objective: Apply Agent SDK hooks for tool call interception and data normalization
question: Your interception hook correctly blocks process_refund calls above the $500 compliance threshold, but it returns a bare "Error: operation failed" to the agent. Production traces show the agent retrying the identical refund three times, then telling customers "our refund system is currently down" — misinformation that generates follow-up tickets. What should change?
options: Add a retry limiter so the agent stops re-attempting after the first blocked refund and moves on to summarizing the conversation
Have the hook return an explicit policy response — refunds above $500 require human approval, use escalate_to_human — so a blocked call becomes a redirect into the correct alternative workflow
Add a system prompt warning that refund attempts above $500 will fail, so the agent learns not to attempt them in the first place
Have the hook return a successful-looking empty result so the agent stops retrying and simply proceeds with the rest of the conversation
optionExplanations: A retry limiter suppresses the symptom while preserving the misdiagnosis: the agent still believes the tool malfunctioned, still tells the customer something false, and still fails to route the case anywhere. The customer's over-threshold refund remains unhandled at the end.

Correct. Interception hooks should not just block — they should redirect to the alternative workflow. A response stating the policy and the correct next step turns the model's reasoning in the right direction: it stops retrying, tells the customer the truthful reason, and escalates for human approval. The block becomes a routed outcome instead of a dead end.

Prompt warnings reduce attempts probabilistically but leave the hook's response broken for every attempt that still occurs — and attempts will occur, since customers state amounts mid-conversation. The deterministic layer must itself communicate usefully; the prompt is a supplement, not the fix.

Returning fake success is silent error suppression: the agent now believes a refund was issued, may confirm that to the customer, and the case closes with a compliance-relevant action falsely recorded as done. This converts a communication defect into a data-integrity incident.
principle: blocked calls should redirect, not dead-end
relatedConcept: Tool call interception pairs blocking with redirection — the hook's response tells the agent why and routes it into the alternative workflow such as human escalation.
overallExplanation: A blocking hook should return an explicit policy response that redirects the agent to the alternative workflow — here, escalation for human approval. Generic errors cause retries and misinformation; fake successes silently corrupt case state.

objective: Apply Agent SDK hooks for tool call interception and data normalization
question: Your developer productivity agent has a delete_records tool that engineers rely on for cleaning test fixtures in the staging environment. A security review demands a hard guarantee that the tool never runs against the production database. The system prompt already forbids production deletes, but the auditors explicitly reject prompt instructions as an acceptable control. What satisfies the requirement while preserving the staging workflow?
options: Implement a tool call interception hook that inspects each delete_records call's target-environment argument and blocks execution against production, redirecting the agent to the manual change-management runbook
Strengthen the system prompt with few-shot examples demonstrating the agent refusing production delete requests in several realistic phrasings
Remove delete_records from the agent entirely and make all fixture cleanup a manual process, since only tool absence fully eliminates the possibility of misuse
Add a PostToolUse hook that pages the security team with full call details whenever a delete completes against the production environment
optionExplanations: Correct. Interception hooks enforce compliance rules on outgoing calls deterministically, and inspecting arguments lets the rule be precise: deletes with a production target are blocked before execution and redirected to the sanctioned manual process, while staging cleanup proceeds untouched. This is the guarantee auditors asked for, scoped so it costs no legitimate functionality.

Few-shot examples lower the probability of a production delete without eliminating it, and the auditors have already ruled that probabilistic controls fail the requirement. Examples are a fine supplement for agent behavior, but they cannot be the control of record for a hard guarantee.

Total removal provides the guarantee but at maximum cost: staging cleanup — the tool's entire legitimate value — reverts to manual work for every engineer. When the dangerous subset of calls is identifiable from arguments, an argument-inspecting block achieves the same guarantee while keeping the tool.

PostToolUse fires after execution: the page arrives when production records are already gone. Alerting after the fact builds an audit trail, which is worthwhile, but the requirement is prevention — the delete must never run, not be promptly regretted.
principle: argument-inspecting interception scopes hard guarantees precisely
relatedConcept: Interception hooks can enforce rules conditioned on a call's arguments — blocking the dangerous subset before execution while leaving legitimate use untouched.
overallExplanation: An interception hook that inspects the target-environment argument blocks production deletes deterministically while preserving staging cleanup. Prompts are probabilistic, tool removal over-pays, and PostToolUse alerts arrive after the damage.

objective: Apply Agent SDK hooks for tool call interception and data normalization
question: During a design workshop for your support agent, four engineers each propose a hook implementation. You want to approve only the proposals that use hooks for what hooks are actually good at, and push the rest toward more appropriate mechanisms. Which two proposals are appropriate uses of Agent SDK hooks? (Choose two.)
options: A PostToolUse hook that converts Unix timestamps, ISO 8601 strings, and numeric status codes arriving from different MCP tools into one consistent format before the model processes them
A hook that parses each assistant message's text and forcibly terminates the agentic loop whenever the phrasing suggests the task sounds finished
An interception hook that blocks process_refund calls exceeding the compliance threshold and redirects those cases into the human escalation workflow
A hook that examines each user message for keywords and dictates which subagent the coordinator must delegate to next based on the matches
optionExplanations: Correct. Normalizing heterogeneous data formats from different MCP tools is the canonical PostToolUse use case: a mechanical, deterministic transformation applied to every result before the model reasons over it, eliminating the intermittent errors that in-context conversion produces.

This launders a named anti-pattern through hook machinery: loop termination decided by parsing natural-language phrasing is unreliable no matter where the parsing code lives. Termination belongs to the structured stop_reason signal — a hook wrapping prose-sniffing is still prose-sniffing.

Correct. Intercepting outgoing tool calls to enforce compliance rules — blocking refunds above a threshold and redirecting to an alternative workflow like human escalation — is precisely the deterministic-guarantee role hooks exist to fill where prompt instructions cannot promise compliance.

Keyword-dictated delegation replaces the coordinator's model-driven judgment with a brittle pre-configured decision tree: routing which subagent handles a query is contextual reasoning the model should perform. Hooks are for deterministic transformations and gates, not for making the agent's decisions.
principle: hooks transform and gate; they do not think for the agent
relatedConcept: Appropriate hook roles are result normalization (PostToolUse) and compliance interception of outgoing calls — not loop control by prose parsing or keyword-driven delegation.
overallExplanation: Hooks earn their keep on deterministic mechanics: PostToolUse normalization of heterogeneous tool data, and interception that blocks policy-violating calls with redirection to escalation. Text-parsed loop termination and keyword-based delegation move model-driven decisions into brittle code.

objective: Design task decomposition strategies for complex workflows
question: Your legal team uses Claude to review 60-page vendor contracts. A single whole-document pass produces sharp findings for early sections and superficial ones later. An engineer then tried per-clause decomposition — over 300 subtasks per contract — which missed obligations that span clauses and multiplied cost. How should the review be decomposed?
options: Keep the per-clause decomposition but batch ten clauses into each request, cutting the subtask count and per-request overhead by an order of magnitude
Decompose per section for focused local analysis, then run a separate cross-section integration pass over the combined findings to catch obligations that span the document
Return to the single whole-document pass with an added instruction to allocate equal analytical depth to every section from the first page to the last
Let the model choose its own decomposition granularity at run time for each contract, since document structure varies and no fixed scheme fits all
optionExplanations: Batching reduces overhead but keeps the structural defect: arbitrary ten-clause windows still sever obligations that reference clauses outside the window, and no pass ever examines the contract's cross-cutting commitments as a whole. The granularity is less extreme but still wrong for the task.

Correct. This applies the local-pass-plus-integration-pass pattern at the right granularity: sections are large enough to give each pass meaningful context, small enough to avoid the attention dilution that degraded the whole-document review, and the dedicated integration pass is where spanning obligations — payment terms referencing termination clauses — get caught by design rather than by luck.

Attention dilution is a property of oversized inputs, not of insufficient willpower: instructing the model to be equally thorough does not restructure the work, and the later-section superficiality will persist. Decomposition, not exhortation, is the fix the first failure already demonstrated.

Contract review is a predictable multi-aspect task — the aspects are known before any contract arrives — which is prompt-chaining territory, not open-ended investigation. Run-time improvised granularity also makes review coverage unauditable, a poor property for a legal workflow.
principle: granularity: big enough for context, small enough for focus, plus integration
relatedConcept: Decomposition granularity is a tradeoff — oversized passes dilute attention, hyper-fine slicing severs cross-cutting concerns — resolved by meaningful chunks plus a dedicated integration pass.
overallExplanation: Decompose at section granularity for focused local passes, then run a cross-section integration pass for spanning obligations. Whole-document passes dilute attention; per-clause slicing severs cross-cutting concerns — both extremes lose findings.

objective: Design task decomposition strategies for complex workflows
question: Your on-call team hands your Agent SDK productivity agent an open-ended assignment: "production latency doubled over the past week — find out why." The cause is genuinely unknown; it could be a code change, an infrastructure shift, data growth, or a dependency update. Which task decomposition approach fits this assignment?
options: A fixed diagnostic pipeline that checks code diffs first, then configuration changes, then dashboards, executed in the same preset order for every incident
A breadth-first sweep that reviews every service in the system in alphabetical order until the anomalous component is eventually encountered
Requiring the on-call engineer to enumerate the complete investigation subtask list up front, so the agent executes a fully specified plan
An adaptive investigation plan: form initial hypotheses, investigate the most likely first, and generate new subtasks based on what each step actually uncovers
optionExplanations: Fixed sequential pipelines fit workflows whose steps are knowable at design time. An unknown-cause incident is the opposite case: a preset order spends its early budget on whichever category the pipeline author guessed first, and the pipeline has no mechanism to pursue the anomaly the first step actually reveals.

Alphabetical order is an arbitrary priority function with no relationship to likelihood of fault: the investigation's early effort lands on whatever sorts first rather than on services implicated by the evidence, and cross-service causes — a shared dependency — may never surface from any single service's review.

This relocates the impossible demand: the cause is unknown to everyone, so the engineer cannot enumerate the right subtasks either. Adaptive decomposition exists precisely so investigation plans can be built incrementally from findings instead of requiring omniscience up front.

Correct. Open-ended investigation is the home ground of dynamic adaptive decomposition: the value of each next step depends on what the last step discovered. Hypothesize, test the most likely, and let findings generate the next subtasks — if the code diff is clean but a dependency bumped mid-week, the plan reshapes around that discovery immediately.
principle: unknown causes demand plans that adapt to findings
relatedConcept: Adaptive investigation plans generate subtasks from what each step discovers — the decomposition pattern for open-ended diagnosis where fixed pipelines investigate the author's guesses.
overallExplanation: An unknown-cause incident calls for dynamic adaptive decomposition: initial hypotheses, likelihood-ordered investigation, and new subtasks generated from each discovery. Fixed pipelines and arbitrary sweeps spend effort on guesses instead of evidence.

objective: Design task decomposition strategies for complex workflows
question: Your team must migrate a large codebase from a legacy logging library to a structured logger. Usage is tangled: some modules call the library directly, others go through home-grown wrapper utilities, and a few construct log calls dynamically. Engineers are debating whether this is a prompt-chaining task or a dynamic-decomposition task. What is the right decomposition design?
options: Combine the patterns: run an exploratory mapping phase to discover usage patterns and high-impact areas, then execute a per-module sequential migration pipeline built from that map, revising the plan when hidden dependencies surface
Treat it as pure prompt chaining: enumerate the module list from a search of import statements and migrate each module in a fixed predetermined order until the list is exhausted
Treat it as pure open-ended investigation: let the agent wander the codebase migrating whatever legacy logging usage it encounters next until no more instances remain
Skip sequencing altogether: spawn parallel subagents immediately, one per top-level directory, and have each migrate its directory's logging calls independently and concurrently
optionExplanations: Correct. The task has an unknowable front half and a predictable back half, so the decomposition should change shape at the boundary: adaptive exploration first — map direct calls, wrappers, and dynamic constructions, identify high-impact areas — then a per-module pipeline whose order and contents come from the map rather than from guesses, kept open to revision as migration surfaces dependencies the map missed.

An import-statement search is exactly what this codebase defeats: wrapper utilities and dynamically constructed calls do not import the legacy library at their call sites, so the enumerated list is incomplete before migration begins. Chaining is right for the execution phase, but only after real discovery builds the list.

Pure wandering forfeits prioritization and coverage guarantees: high-impact shared wrappers might be migrated last, the agent cannot say what remains at any point, and completion is asserted rather than known. Once mapping is done, this task's execution is predictable — squandering that predictability is a design error.

Immediate parallelization before mapping collides at the shared seams: multiple subagents will each encounter the same cross-directory wrapper utilities and migrate them independently, producing conflicting edits. Parallel execution may be viable later, but only after the map reveals where the shared surfaces are.
principle: explore to build the map; chain to execute it
relatedConcept: Hybrid decomposition — an adaptive mapping phase feeding a structured execution pipeline — fits tasks whose discovery is open-ended but whose execution becomes predictable once mapped.
overallExplanation: Map first, then chain: exploratory discovery of usage patterns and high-impact areas builds the module plan, and a sequential per-module pipeline executes it, adapting when hidden dependencies surface. Static searches miss wrappers and dynamic calls; wandering forfeits coverage guarantees.

objective: Design task decomposition strategies for complex workflows
question: You are writing your platform team's decomposition playbook for agent workloads, matching each recurring workflow to the decomposition pattern it should use. Reviewers will reject any pairing that misapplies a pattern. Which two pairings are correct? (Choose two.)
options: Prompt chaining for the recurring pull-request review, whose aspects — per-file local analysis followed by cross-file integration checking — are known before any PR arrives
Dynamic adaptive decomposition for the nightly report job, which always runs the same three steps of gathering metrics, formatting tables, and publishing the summary
Prompt chaining for diagnosing an intermittent crash that no one can reproduce, so the investigation follows a dependable predetermined sequence
Dynamic adaptive decomposition for exploring an undocumented legacy system, where each finding determines which component deserves examination next
optionExplanations: Correct. PR review is a predictable multi-aspect task: every review needs per-file local passes and a cross-file integration pass, and this structure is known at design time. Prompt chaining encodes it as a fixed sequence of focused steps, giving repeatable coverage without attention dilution.

A three-step job that never varies is the strongest possible case for a fixed pipeline — adaptive decomposition here adds nondeterminism, cost, and failure modes to a workflow with nothing to adapt to. Reserving dynamic patterns for tasks with genuine unknowns is the playbook's whole point.

An unreproducible intermittent crash is the canonical unknown: the next useful step depends entirely on what the last probe revealed, so no predetermined sequence can be dependable. Assigning prompt chaining here investigates the sequence author's guesses instead of the evidence.

Correct. Undocumented legacy exploration is open-ended investigation: structure, risk areas, and dependencies are discovered rather than known, so the plan must generate subtasks from findings. Dynamic adaptive decomposition — map, prioritize, adapt as dependencies emerge — is the matching pattern.
principle: pattern follows predictability: chain the knowable, adapt to the unknown
relatedConcept: Prompt chaining suits workflows whose aspects are enumerable at design time; dynamic decomposition suits investigations whose subtasks emerge from findings.
overallExplanation: Match the pattern to task predictability: prompt chaining for enumerable multi-aspect work like per-file-plus-integration PR review, and dynamic adaptive decomposition for open-ended exploration like undocumented legacy systems. Fixed jobs need no adaptivity; unreproducible mysteries defeat fixed sequences.

objective: Manage session state, resumption, and forking
question: An engineer on your team runs several long-running Claude Code investigations concurrently — an authentication bug hunt and a performance audit — each spanning multiple days. Every morning she launches a fresh claude session and spends the first half hour re-explaining the codebase areas involved and re-establishing what each investigation has already ruled out. What practice eliminates this daily overhead?
options: Consolidate both investigations into one perpetual session that is never closed, so all accumulated context stays available in a single place
Record each investigation's findings in the project CLAUDE.md file so every new session automatically loads the current state of both efforts
Give each investigation a named session and continue the right one each morning with --resume <session-name>, restoring that conversation's accumulated context intact
End each day by copying the final assistant message into a notes file, then paste it into the next morning's fresh session as the opening message
optionExplanations: A single perpetual session interleaves two unrelated investigations, so each morning's work wades through the other effort's tool results and reasoning — and the combined context fills far faster. Merged history is barely an improvement on no history when the concerns are distinct.

CLAUDE.md is configuration — standards and conventions loaded into every session — not a journal of in-flight investigation state. Stuffing daily findings into it pollutes shared team context, burdens every unrelated session with both investigations' notes, and still loses the conversational reasoning chain.

Correct. Named session resumption exists for exactly this: --resume <session-name> continues a specific prior conversation, so "auth-bug" and "perf-audit" each persist as separate threads with their accumulated exploration, ruled-out hypotheses, and tool results intact. The half hour of morning reconstruction simply disappears.

One final assistant message is a keyhole view of a multi-day investigation: everything not restated in that last message — earlier findings, dead ends, file-level details — is lost, and the morning still begins with re-exploration. Manual transcript shuttling is the workaround named sessions obsolete.
principle: one named session per investigation; --resume continues it
relatedConcept: Named session resumption with --resume <session-name> continues a specific prior conversation across work sessions, keeping concurrent investigations separate and intact.
overallExplanation: Name each investigation's session and continue it with --resume <session-name> — each thread's accumulated context returns intact, with concurrent efforts kept separate. Perpetual merged sessions, CLAUDE.md journaling, and pasted final messages all lose or pollute context.

objective: Manage session state, resumption, and forking
question: After an expensive session in which Claude Code built a deep analysis of your service's architecture, the team wants to evaluate two candidate testing strategies — property-based testing versus snapshot testing — with each evaluation grounded in that analysis but conducted independently, so neither exploration's conclusions influence the other. What is the right session-management approach?
options: Evaluate both strategies sequentially inside the resumed session, instructing the model to disregard the first evaluation entirely before beginning the second
Use fork_session to create two independent branches from the shared analysis baseline, exploring one testing strategy in each branch
Start two brand-new sessions and have each rebuild the architecture analysis from scratch before evaluating its assigned strategy
Resume the same named session in two terminals at once and run one strategy evaluation in each, letting the shared name keep them synchronized
optionExplanations: Instructing a model to disregard prior context does not remove it: the first strategy's reasoning, tradeoffs, and partial conclusions remain in the conversation and bias the second evaluation. Sequential evaluation in one thread is precisely the cross-contamination the team said it must avoid.

Correct. fork_session exists for exploring divergent approaches from a shared analysis baseline: both branches inherit the expensive architecture analysis once, then diverge completely, so each strategy is evaluated on identical footing with no leakage between explorations. Comparing testing strategies from a shared baseline is the pattern's textbook application.

Independence is achieved, but the expensive analysis is paid for twice — and worse, the two rebuilt analyses may differ in coverage or emphasis, so the strategy comparison is no longer conducted against the same baseline. Forking delivers the same independence while preserving both cost and comparability.

This treats a session name as a synchronization mechanism, which it is not — the name identifies one conversation thread, and pushing two divergent evaluations into it produces interleaved, mutually contaminating context rather than parallel isolation. Branching is fork_session's job.

relatedConcept: fork_session creates independent branches from a shared analysis baseline — the mechanism for comparing testing or refactoring strategies without cross-contamination or re-analysis cost.
overallExplanation: fork_session branches the expensive shared analysis into independent explorations — one per testing strategy — with identical baselines and zero cross-contamination. Sequential evaluation contaminates; rebuilding pays twice and breaks comparability.

question: Two sprints ago you built a rich Claude Code session analyzing your order-management service. Resuming the old session today, the agent confidently describes module boundaries and call paths that no longer exist. How should the investigation be continued?

Resume the old session and enumerate all forty changed files so the agent performs targeted re-analysis of each before continuing the investigation
Resume the old session unchanged and rely on its accumulated history, since a rich conversation record always outweighs some staleness in tool results
Use fork_session to branch the old session into a fresh copy, since forking discards the parent's stale tool results while preserving its conclusions

When prior tool results are broadly stale, starting fresh with an injected structured summary is the more reliable pattern: curated, still-valid conclusions carry forward as explicit context, while everything about current code structure comes from new tool calls against the real codebase. The confident-but-wrong answers disappear because their stale source material is gone.

Targeted re-analysis is the right move when a couple of known files changed; at forty files across multiple branches it approximates full re-exploration while the resumed history still holds stale results for anything the enumeration misses — and those remain in context, ready to resurface as confident errors.

The observed behavior already falsifies this: stale tool results are worse than absent ones because the agent treats them as current ground truth. When most of the analyzed area has changed, accumulated history is a liability describing a codebase that no longer exists.

This misstates what forking does: fork_session branches a session to explore divergent approaches from a shared baseline, and the branch inherits that baseline — including every stale tool result. Forking is for parallel exploration, not a cleansing mechanism for outdated context.

question: A newly drafted onboarding document for your platform team makes four claims about Claude Code session management, and you have been asked to strike the inaccurate ones before it circulates. Which two claims are accurate and should stay in the document? (Choose two.)
options: Resumed sessions automatically detect files changed since the last turn and silently refresh any stale tool results in the conversation history
When resuming a session after code modifications, you should tell the agent which previously analyzed files changed so it can re-analyze them targetedly
Choose resumption when prior context is mostly valid; when old tool results are broadly stale, start a fresh session seeded with a structured summary instead
When forked branches complete, fork_session automatically merges each branch's findings back into the parent session for consolidated review

This misbelief is dangerous precisely because it removes the practice — informing the agent of changes — that actually mitigates staleness.

Correct. Informing a resumed session about specific file changes is the documented practice: it directs targeted re-analysis at exactly the stale parts, preserving the rest of the accumulated investigation instead of forcing full re-exploration or silently trusting outdated results.

Correct. This is the core resumption decision rule: resumption pays off when the saved context is mostly still true, while broadly stale tool results make a fresh session with an injected structured summary the more reliable continuation — curated knowledge forward, ground truth rebuilt.
